NPJ9KZqrl50: In 1740, while Swiss naturalist Abraham Trembley was tutoring the sons of a nobleman, he had scooped up some pond water for them to study when he found something shocking inside. He couldn't identify the odd little thing or even tell if it was a plant or an animal. Its way of moving and consuming things seemed animal-like. But when he cut parts off, or even split it in two, it regenerated, which was decidedly plant-like, in keeping with its green hue. Trembley noted the organism’s similarity to the Hydra, the monster from Greek mythology, and the name stuck. Today, we know hydras are animals capable of some incredible feats, apparently including immortality. They comprise a genus of tiny aquatic animals in the broader phylum Cnidaria. Some cnidarians, like jellyfish, have a stationary polyp phase, then a free-swimming Medusa stage. But hydras and some of their relatives stay polyps their whole lives. Hydras have relatively simple cylindrical body plans, one end forming the foot, the other the mouth, framed by fanning tentacles. They’ll eat just about any critter they can snag. And although they can scoot around if needed, most of the time, they remain stuck to things using a gluey substance secreted from their foot. They can reproduce sexually, but they more often do so asexually, budding new growths off their bodies. Where exactly they hunker down in the freshwater ponds and slow-moving streams they populate varies by species, which likewise differ in shape, size, and hue. Green hydras, for one, bask in sunny spots to feed the photosynthetic algae they host, which lend them their color and provide sugars in return for other nutrients.
